CANONICAL_NAME.value: SPDY (spdylay) -- the experimental protocol that became HTTP/2 and was then retired

ERA.value: 2009-2015 (SPDY); HTTP/2 published 2015; SPDY removed from Chrome 2016

value.lineage: SPDY (Google, 2009) attacked HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking with multiplexed streams, header compression and prioritisation over one TLS connection. It worked, and the IETF took it as the BASIS for HTTP/2 (RFC 7540). Its authors then deprecated it: SPDY is a loser of an unusual kind -- defeated by its own successor, having won the argument. spdylay is Tatsuhiro Tsujikawa's C implementation (the ancestor of nghttp2).

value.built_to: remove HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking by multiplexing many requests over one connection with compressed headers
value.pressure: pages needing dozens of round-trips over high-latency links; browsers opening many TCP connections to work around it
value.success_means: fewer connections and lower page load time at the same bandwidth

value.pressure: latency and connection limits; TCP head-of-line blocking under loss
value.failure_condition: retired by its own authors once its ideas were standardised as HTTP/2; deployments moved off it

evidence.says: HTTP/2 was developed from SPDY as its starting point and supersedes it as the standardised protocol.
Google announced it would remove SPDY support from Chrome in favour of HTTP/2.

cut.note: the three SPDY ideas that HTTP/2 inherited, each visible as a data structure: streams multiplexed on one connection with a per-stream priority that orders a priority queue of outbound frames (control frames such as PING and SETTINGS jump the queue by fixed priorities; SYN_STREAMs keep insertion order at the lowest priority); header compression by deflate with a shared pre-seeded dictionary of common header names and values (one per protocol version); and per-stream plus per-connection flow-control windows updated by WINDOW_UPDATE frames

provenance.grade_basis: Techne FOSSIL_PACKET.json PROVENANCE_GRADE where issued, else the record's handoff string mapped (populated per R34; Harmonia may re-grade)

organs.human_name: spdylay_session_add_frame (357-420): item->seq, item->pri per frame type (PING SPDYLAY_OB_PRI_PING, SETTINGS -1, SYN_REPLY / RST_STREAM / HEADERS the stream's pri, SYN_STREAM lowest); ob_pq and ob_ss_pq (202-206); spdylay_outbound_item_compar (99); the pop logic 1025-1097
organs.mechanism: every frame to send becomes an outbound item with a sequence number and a priority; the priority is the stream's for frames belonging to an open stream, a fixed high value for PING, a fixed value for SETTINGS, and the lowest for new SYN_STREAMs, which also go to a separate queue so that stream openings are sent in the order requested and never starve data; the sender pops the higher-priority head of the two queues (ties broken by sequence), so a client's priority hints translate directly into transmission order on the single TLS connection
organs.input: frames from the application and the protocol
assumptions: the application's priorities are meaningful; control frames must not wait behind data (a stalled PING would look like a dead connection)
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: head-of-line blocking of HTTP/1.1 removed without multiple connections; the priority model HTTP/2 refined into a dependency tree
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: priorities are absolute integers, so a low-priority stream can starve indefinitely behind a busy high one (HTTP/2's weighted tree was the answer); the two-queue split is a workaround for SYN_STREAM ordering
organs.human_prior: SPDY draft 2/3 (Google 2009-2012); RFC 7540 section 5.3 for the successor
organs.source_boundary: add_frame, the compare function and the pop path

organs.human_name: spdylay_zlib.c: spdy2_hd_dict (33), spdy3_hd_dict (48), spdylay_select_hd_dict (229-240); deflate / inflate with SetDictionary
organs.mechanism: each direction of a session keeps a zlib stream for header blocks; the stream is primed with a fixed dictionary containing the header names and values that appear in nearly every request (methods, status codes, common header names, dates), so even the first request's headers compress well; SPDY/2 and SPDY/3 have different dictionaries; the compressor state persists across frames, so repeated headers cost almost nothing
assumptions: headers are highly redundant across requests; a shared prefix dictionary fixes the cold-start cost
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: request headers shrink by most of their size; the mechanism HTTP/2 REPLACED (with HPACK) because compressing secrets alongside attacker-controlled bytes leaks them (CRIME, 2012)
organs.failure_landscape: by reading: the compression context is shared across streams of one connection, which is exactly the CRIME side channel; the body predates the fix
organs.human_prior: deflate with a preset dictionary (zlib's deflateSetDictionary)

organs.human_name: spdylay_session_on_window_update_received (1877), update_initial_window_size (1745), update_recv_window_size / recv_connection_window_size (2359-2382), predicate_window_update_send (708), add_window_update (2776)
organs.mechanism: each stream carries a send window decremented by the data it sends and a receive window decremented by what it receives; the receiver sends WINDOW_UPDATE when its consumed bytes cross a threshold, and the sender may not send data beyond its window; SPDY/3 added a connection-level window over all streams; a SETTINGS change of the initial window size adjusts every open stream's window by the difference
organs.input: DATA frames; WINDOW_UPDATE and SETTINGS frames
organs.state: window sizes per stream and per session
assumptions: receiver-driven credit is the right control when many streams share one TCP connection (TCP's own window is per connection, so one slow consumer would stall all)
organs.fitness_value_in_ancestor: one stalled stream no longer blocks the others; the same design in HTTP/2 section 6.9
organs.source_boundary: the window functions; CANDIDATE because read by name

rejected_cuts.candidate: the frame encoder/decoder (spdylay_frame.c), the stream state machine (spdylay_stream.c), the receive path and its callbacks (mem_recv 2474-2738), NPN negotiation, the map / pq / buffer containers, the shrpx proxy and examples, the tests

rejected_cuts.evidence: multiplexing with priorities, header compression and flow control are separable and HTTP/2 kept two, replaced one and refined the third

pressures.source_evidence: spdylay_session.c add_frame and the queues; spdylay_zlib.c dictionaries; the window functions
pressures.condition: an organism carries N concurrent request/response exchanges over one reliable ordered byte stream; consumers drain at different rates; each exchange carries hundreds of bytes of mostly repeated headers; the score is page-load latency and bytes on the wire
pressures.resource_or_constraint: one connection; a compression context per direction
pressures.failure_condition: head-of-line blocking (one slow stream delays the rest) or header bytes dominating small requests
pressures.world_punishes: one exchange at a time; per-request compression from a cold context
pressures.world_rewards: multiplexed frames with priorities, per-stream credit windows, a persistent compressor with a seeded dictionary
pressures.observable_consequence: page-load time and header bytes for a page of 50 resources over HTTP/1.1 (6 connections) vs SPDY over one connection, with one resource's consumer stalled
pressures.trivial_shortcuts: many parallel connections (which the world may cap, as browsers did)
pressures.cheat_control: an organism with unlimited connections must match SPDY's latency at higher connection count; serial HTTP/1.1 must show the head-of-line delay; SPDY with the dictionary removed must show the cold-start header cost: the world must show all three
pressures.purpose_separated_from_pressure: PURPOSE: multiplexed HTTP transport (Google SPDY 2009; spdylay 2012-)
